procedural_history.impugned_order: The Industrial Tribunal ordered reinstatement with half of back wages after finding the employee guilty of misconduct.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The employer approached the High Court under Article 227 to quash the reinstatement order. The High Court vacated the reinstatement order and quantified compensation at Rs. 15,000.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The workman appealed to the Supreme Court after obtaining leave under Article 136 of the Constitution, challenging the High Court's decision.

directions: The order of the High Court is set aside and the award of the Industrial Tribunal is restored.
The appellant would be entitled to full wages and other service benefits from December 24, 1979.
The appellant would also be entitled to the half of the back wages in terms of the award from May 14, 1977 till December 23, 1979.
We direct the Tribunal to compute the amount so due as back wages and the appellant is entitled to 12 per cent interest on the sum from January 1, 1980, till payment.
The appeal is allowed with costs. Hearing fee assessed at Rs. 2000.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution, is justified in interfering with an Industrial Tribunal's award by vacating an order of reinstatement and substituting it with quantified compensation, particularly when the Tribunal has exercised its discretion under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.

facts: An employee's services were terminated for misconduct.
The Industrial Tribunal found the charge of misconduct was established but concluded that the punishment of termination was not warranted.
Exercising its discretion under the Industrial Disputes Act, the Tribunal ordered the employee's reinstatement with half of his back wages.
The employer challenged this award in the High Court under Article 227 of the Constitution.
The High Court vacated the Tribunal's order of reinstatement and substituted it with a compensation award of Rs. 15,000.
law: Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, vests wide discretion in the Industrial Tribunal to award relief according to the circumstances of the case.
The High Court, under its supervisory jurisdiction in Article 227, does not possess the same wide discretion as the Tribunal.
The High Court's power under Article 227 is one of superintendence, allowing it to scrutinize orders of subordinate tribunals within well-accepted limitations.

A High Court can quash a tribunal's award and remit the matter for fresh disposal, but it is not entitled to exercise the powers of the tribunal and substitute its own award, as it would in an appeal.
application: The Supreme Court determined that the Industrial Tribunal had properly exercised its wide discretion under Section 11A by ordering reinstatement, even after finding misconduct.
It held that the High Court overstepped its limited supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 by acting as an appellate court.
The Court stated that it is ordinarily "not for the High Court in exercise of the jurisdiction of superintendence to substitute one finding for another and similarly one punishment for another."

The Supreme Court found that the High Court had "no justification to interfere" with the reinstatement order and that its decision to substitute it with quantified compensation was "erroneous both on facts and in law" and lacked any "legitimate basis."
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's interference. It held that the High Court was not justified in substituting the Industrial Tribunal's discretionary award of reinstatement with monetary compensation. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and restored the original award of the Industrial Tribunal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227 of the Constitution, is justified in interfering with an Industrial Tribunal's award by vacating an order of reinstatement and substituting it with quantified compensation, particularly when the Tribunal has exercised its discretion under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's modification of the Tribunal's award is being assailed.
The Industrial Tribunal is vested with wide discretion under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and can order reinstatement even if misconduct is established.
The High Court, in substituting the reinstatement order with compensation, acted without any legitimate basis and overstepped its supervisory jurisdiction under Article 227.
respondent_arguments: Since the Industrial Tribunal found the workman guilty of misconduct, it was obligatory for the Tribunal to impose a punishment other than reinstatement.
The High Court was justified in quashing the direction of reinstatement because a finding of misconduct had been made against the workman.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Under its power of superintendence (Article 227), a High Court is not entitled to exercise the wide discretionary powers vested in an Industrial Tribunal under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The High Court cannot substitute its own award or punishment for that of the Tribunal; its proper role is to quash an erroneous award and remit the matter back to the Tribunal for fresh disposal.
obiter: The court may not have denied the High Court the power to substitute a finding or punishment in every type of case.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's interference with the Industrial Tribunal's award was unjustified. The High Court's approach was deemed 'totally uncalled for' and its decision to vacate the reinstatement order and substitute it with compensation was 'erroneous both on facts and in law.' The Court concluded that the High Court acted without any legitimate basis in overturning the Tribunal's discretionary order, especially when the Tribunal, exercising its powers under Section 11A, had determined that reinstatement would meet the ends of justice.
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 11A of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, wide discretion is vested in the Tribunal, which can vacate an order of dismissal or discharge and give suitable directions based on the established facts of the case.
Ordinarily, it is not for the High Court, in the exercise of its jurisdiction of superintendence under Article 227, to substitute one finding for another and similarly one punishment for another.
policy_considerations: The High Court failed to consider whether there was a 'loss of confidence' by the employer, a relevant factor for denying reinstatement. The Court noted that the job of a librarian does not inherently involve the necessity of enjoying any special confidence of the employer.

When substituting reinstatement with compensation, the High Court failed to consider crucial factors for a fair calculation, such as how many years of service the appellant had completed, how many years of service were left, and the salary and other service benefits the appellant was receiving.
